abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Voriconazole is the cornerstone of the treatment and prevention of fungal infections. While there is a good correlation between CYP2C19 genotype and voriconazole exposure during prophylactic treatment, no correlation was found in patients with invasive aspergillosis. Proinflammatory cytokines result in inhibition of CYP2C19 enzyme activity (and may result in phenoconversion). Here we investigated the relationship between inflammation, CYP2C19 genotype‐predicted‐phenotype, and CYP2C19 activity in patients receiving voriconazole. Data were obtained from two prospective studies investigating voriconazole treatment (NCT02074462 and NCT00893555). Dose‐corrected voriconazole plasma concentration and C‐reactive protein (CRP) were used as proxies for CYP2C19 activity and inflammation, respectively. After data extraction and synthesis, data from 39 patients with paired voriconazole and CRP measurements were available. The distribution of CYP2C19 genotype‐predicted metabolizer phenotypes was 31% intermediate (IM), 41% normal (NM), and 28% rapid metabolizer (RM). During inflammation, dose‐corrected voriconazole levels were increased by 245%, 278%, and 486% for CYP2C19 NMs IMs and RMs, respectively. Patients with moderate or high CRP levels (>50 mg/L) were phenoconverted to a lower metabolizer phenotype irrespective of their CYP2C19 genotype. In a subgroup analysis of eight patients with longitudinal data available with and without inflammation, the pattern of the dose‐corrected voriconazole and CRP measurements were similar, with CYP2C19 activity following decreasing or increasing CRP levels. In conclusion, voriconazole plasma concentrations increase during inflammation due to downregulation of CYP2C19 activity. While this effect appears largest for CYP2C19 RMs, no clinically relevant differences were observed between the CYP2C19 genotypes.

p.bold: WHAT IS THE CURRENT KNOWLEDGE ON THE TOPIC?

boxed-text.p:
The antifungal voriconazole is widely used both in the prophylactic and therapeutic treatment of stem cell transplantation recipients. While there is a good correlation between CYP2C19 genotype and voriconazole exposure in the prophylactic setting, no such correlation was found in patients with invasive aspergillosis.
WHAT QUESTION DID THIS STUDY ADDRESS?

Here we investigated if inflammation influences CYP2C19 activity differently with respect to the CYP2C19 genotype‐predicted drug metabolizer phenotype using voriconazole exposure as a proxy.
WHAT DOES THIS STUDY ADD TO OUR KNOWLEDGE?

In patients with increased c‐reactive protein (CRP) levels, the CYP2C19 genotype to phenotype relation is disrupted and patients with higher CRP levels can be phenoconverted to a lower CYP2C19 metabolizer phenotype than indicated by their genotype.
HOW MIGHT THIS CHANGE CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY OR TRANSLATIONAL SCIENCE?
Inflammation presents an important source of phenoconversion. The level of inflammation may be considered when using genotype‐predicted drug metabolizer phenotypes to guide drug dosing.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Voriconazole treatment is both used in the prophylactic setting and as therapeutic treatment for invasive fungal infections. These infections are a significant complication after allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation and cause severe morbidity and mortality. 1 , 2 Voriconazole is characterized by complex pharmacokinetics with substantial inter‐ and intrapatient variability and nonlinear kinetics. Therefore, therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is used to attain the target trough concentration of 1–6 mg/L. 3

Voriconazole is mainly converted into inactive metabolites by the cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme 2C19. 4 In addition, CYP3A4, CYP2C9, and flavin‐containing monooxygenases are also involved in the metabolism of voriconazole. 5 The gene encoding CYP2C19 is polymorphic. Both decreased function e.g. *2, *3 and increased function, for example, *17 alleles have been described. Five drug metabolizer phenotypes are distinguished: poor (PM), intermediate (IM), normal (NM), rapid (RM), and ultra‐rapid (UM) metabolizers. 6 , 7 In people of European descent, the phenotype frequencies are 2% PM, 23% IM, 47% NM, 26% RM, and 2% UM. However, depending on ancestry phenotype frequencies can vary considerably. For example, ~60% of the Asian are PM and IM. 8 The Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) recommends to starting with the standard voriconazole dose for CYP2C19 NMs and IMs. For RMs, Ums, and PMs an alternative treatment is recommended. 6 The Dutch Pharmacogenetics Working Group guidelines recommend starting voriconazole treatment with 50% of the normal dose in CYP2C19 PMs and 150% in CYP2C19 UMs. Two prospective studies investigating CYP2C19‐guided dosing in patients receiving voriconazole prophylaxis confirmed a clear correlation between the RM and UM genotype and lower voriconazole levels. 9 , 10 CYP2C19 UMs and RMs achieved therapeutic drug levels with 300 mg voriconazole twice daily versus 200 mg twice daily for NM, IM, and PM. 9 , 10

However, in contrast to the prophylactic setting, results from a recently published prospective trial in patients (n = 189) with invasive aspergilloses showed no correlation between CYP2C19 genotype and voriconazole levels. 11 Inflammation‐induced phenoconversion has been suggested as an explanation for the lack of correlation between CYP2C19 genotype and voriconazole concentration in patients with inflammation. 12 , 13 During inflammation, proinflammatory cytokines are released that reduce mRNA levels of CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 via different signaling pathways, for example, JAK/STAT or C/EBPα, resulting in decreased CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 expression and enzyme activity. 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 Indeed, CYP2C19 activity can be down‐regulated by the proinflammatory cytokines tumor necrosis factor (TNF)‐α, interleukin (IL)‐1β, IL‐6, IL‐2, and interferon (IFN)‐γ. 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 Moreover, upregulation of IL‐6 was found to decrease CYP activity in general in patients with inflammation, 21 , 22 and voriconazole levels increased in patients that developed an invasive fungal infection. 23 , 24 , 25
Here we investigate the relationship between inflammation, CYP2C19 genotype‐predicted metabolizer phenotype, and CYP2C19 activity in patients with and without inflammation receiving voriconazole.

sec.title: Study subjects
sec.p: Data were obtained from two prospective studies. The first was a prospective observational study of patients receiving voriconazole at the University Medical Center Groningen (UMCG) (NCT02074462). 26 The second study was a multicenter prospective stratified cluster randomized cross‐over trial of TDM in hematology patients receiving voriconazole for the treatment of invasive aspergillosis (VORIZONMW trial NCT00893555). 11 The inclusion criteria for the current study were: (1) participation with consent for follow‐up studies in NCT02074462 or NCT00893555, (2) over 18 years of age, (3) treated with voriconazole >24 h after two loading doses or at least 10 doses of voriconazole, (4) available CYP2C19 genotype, (5) paired (same day) voriconazole trough (C min) and C‐reactive protein (CRP) levels.

sec.title: Analyses
sec.p: The primary analysis investigated the relationship between inflammation and CYP2C19 activity. Secondary analysis explored whether the occurrence of inflammation‐induced phenoconversion differed per CYP2C19 genotype‐predicted metabolizer phenotype. Phenoconversion was defined as a change in CYP2C19 activity during inflammation resulting in a CYP2C19 activity that corresponds to the CYP2C19 activity of a less active CYP2C19 drug metabolizer phenotype without inflammation. For example, during inflammation, a genotype‐predicted CYP2C19 RM shows the CYP2C19 activity of a genotype‐predicted CYP2C19 IM without inflammation.

In a subgroup analysis with low and increased inflammation, it was investigated how inflammation and voriconazole levels correlate to each other over time by analyzing trends in dose‐corrected voriconazole and CRP levels.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: Data included age, sex, weight, voriconazole trough concentration, dose, and route of administration, concomitant use of interacting CYP450 medications. Dose‐corrected voriconazole C min levels were calculated via [1‐voriconazole concentration (mg/L)/voriconazole dose (mg)] and used as a proxy for CYP2C19 activity. For recipients of a stem cell transplant, DNA was isolated prior transplantation. CYP2C19 genotyping was performed at the LUMC as part of the original study protocols. In brief genotyping was performed using a TaqMan assay with predesigned probes for CYP2C19 *2, *3 and *17 and carried out according to the manufacturer's instructions [TaqMan® genotyping assays by Thermofisher (Waltham, MA, USA)]. The CYP2C19 genotype results were translated into predicted drug metabolizer phenotypes based on CPIC recommendations (PM, IM, NM, RM, or UM, Table S1). 6 Voriconazole concentrations were measured with a validated LC–MS/MS method as described in detail previously. 27 The limit of quantification was 0.1 mg/L.

sec.title: Inflammation
sec.p: CRP is produced by the liver in response of increased IL‐6 levels. CRP levels are an accepted proxy for the level of inflammation (12–14). Inflammation was defined as a CRP level >10 mg/L. Based on the clinical guidelines, different levels of inflammation were defined as follows: “low” CRP 10–51 mg/L, “moderate” CRP 52–100 mg/L, and “severe” CRP >100 mg/L. 28 , 29 CRP and voriconazole through levels were acquired on the same day.

sec.title: Data analysis & statistics
sec.p: Continuous variables were summarized as the median and range, predicted drug metabolizer phenotype and inflammation groups were summarized as mean and standard error of means, and nominal variables as the number and percentage. Longitudinal data on the voriconazole dose‐corrected concentration were analyzed using a linear regression model. All statistical analyses were performed using Rstudio (version 4.1.0).

sec.title: RESULTS
sec.p: After data extraction and synthesis, the dataset for the primary analysis contained 39 patients with paired voriconazole and CRP measurements (Figure 1). 11 , 26 Of these, 26 (66%) were males. The patients had a median age of 61 years, median weight of 76 kg and median length of 178 cm (Table 1). Most patients received voriconazole as part of the stem cell transplantation protocol for leukemia (77%). Most of the patients were categorized as CYP2C19 NM (n = 16; 41%), 10 were IMs (26%), 10 were RMs (26%), and two were UMs (5%). No PMs were observed. The mean dose‐corrected voriconazole trough and CRP levels were 3.32 and 89.7 mg/L, respectively. Most of the times voriconazole was administered orally (81% of the measurements). Concomitant treatment with CYP2C19 substrates such as pantoprazole or moderate CYP2C19 inhibitors such as omeprazole occurred in 59% (Table 2).

The number of voriconazole trough levels per patient ranged from 1–60 measurements for the primary, 2–60 measurements for the secondary analysis, and 4–42 measurements for the subgroup analysis.

sec.p: The results of the primary analysis show that the dose‐corrected voriconazole level increased with increasing CRP concentration (Figure 2). There was a significant positive association between dose‐corrected voriconazole trough concentration and CRP (β = 3.262e‐05, R 2 = 0.1634 p = < 0.001).

caption.p: Relation between CRP plasma concentration and dose‐corrected voriconazole level. The line represents the regression of all samples (y = 4.995e‐03 + 3.262e‐05x, p = < 0.001).

sec.p: The number of available voriconazole trough and CRP levels varied substantially between patients and ranged from 2 to 60. To investigate the effect of the number of measurements per patient, a sensitivity analysis was performed. The results showed no significant effect of the number of measurement per patient on the relation between CRP and dose‐corrected voriconazole trough level (Figures S1 and S2).

The secondary analysis explored the effect of inflammation on phenoconversion for the different CYP2C19 genotype‐predicted metabolizer phenotypes. For this analysis only patients with multiple voriconazole measurements were included. Consequently, four patients with single measurements were excluded. The CYP2C19 activities measured during and without severe inflammation were compared and stratified for CYP2C19 genotype‐predicted drug metabolizer phenotype. Since, there was only one subject with UM phenotype with multiple measurements, this subject was excluded from the analysis. As expected, the CYP2C19 activity, transformed dose‐corrected voriconazole levels, without inflammation was higher for RMs (measured CYP2C19 enzyme activity 0.998 ± 0.000228) compared with NMs (measured CYP2C19 enzyme activity 0.995 ± 0.000141) and IMs (measured CYP2C19 enzyme activity 0.995 ± 0.000403). The activity decreased for all CYP2C19 predicted drug metabolizer phenotypes at higher inflammatory status (CRP > 100 mg/L). During severe inflammation, the CYP2C19 activity of IM, NM, and RM were similar to the CYP2C19 activity of a lower metabolizer phenotype in the absence of inflammation. The largest effect of inflammation on CYP2C19 activity was observed for the RM phenotype, and the smallest effect for the NMs. For CYP2C19 NMs the increase in dose‐corrected voriconazole level was 245%, for IMs 278% and for RMs 486% (Table 3).

sec.p: We observed the decrease to a similarly low CYP2C19 activity range for all CYP2C19 predicted drug metabolizer phenotypes during inflammation. Since dichotomizing inflammation may be an oversimplification, we performed an exploratory analysis by splitting the CRP measurements between 10 and 100 mg/L in a low (CRP 10–51 mg/L) and moderate (52–100 mg/L) inflammation group. This analysis indicates that the RMs at low inflammation level show comparable measured CYP2C19 activity to NM and IM genotype‐predicted drug metabolizer phenotypes without inflammation (Figure 3). At moderate inflammation for all metabolizer phenotype groups (IM, NM, and RM) the measured CYP2C19 activity is already lower than the NM and IM level in the absence of inflammation. Additionally, at the moderate inflammation level, the measured CYP2C19 activity of all CYP2C19 predicted drug metabolizer phenotype groups were decreased to a level lower than IMs without inflammation.

sec.p: For a subgroup of eight patients voriconazole levels and CRP levels were available in absence and presence of inflammation. With the data from these patients, we explored if the change in dose‐corrected voriconazole trough level and CRP was different for the several CYP2C19 phenotypes (Figure 4). Voriconazole and CRP levels followed similar patterns with higher voriconazole levels with increasing CRP and vice‐versa in all patients (Figure 4A1,A2,B2,B3,C1,C2). As expected, dose‐corrected voriconazole trough levels were highest for IMs and lowest for RMs in the absence of inflammation (Figure 4A3,B3,C1). During inflammation, no large difference in the dose‐corrected voriconazole trough levels of the different drug metabolizer phenotypes were observed, the highest levels were detected in NMs (Figure 4B2,B3).

caption.p: Effect of inflammation on voriconazole pharmacokinetics in the subgroup of subjects with data prior to and during inflammation. This figure shows the dose‐corrected voriconazole (red) and C‐reactive protein (CRP) levels (blue) for patients with a voriconazole trough level in without (CPR < 10) and with (CRP ≥ 10) inflammation presented by predicted CYP2C19 phenotype, three CYP2C19‐predicted intermediate metabolizers (a), three CYP2C19‐predicted normal metabolizers (b), two CYP1C19‐predicted rapid metabolizers (c). Measurements are sequential, but information regarding the intervals is lacking.

sec.p: To explore the impact of inflammation on voriconazole target attainment in the subgroup, we plotted the voriconazole trough concentration against CRP level and dosage (Figure S3A1,A3,B1,B2,B3,C1,C2). As expected, IMs required a lower dose compared with NMs and RMs to reach target levels in the absence of inflammation. Out of the 110 available voriconazole measurements, 18 were outside the therapeutic target range (16%), of which four were supratherapeutic (Figure S3). Interestingly, all supratherapeutic levels occurred during inflammation.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: The current study investigated the association of CYP2C19 genotype‐predicted drug metabolizer phenotype and CYP2C19 activity in patients receiving voriconazole in the absence and presence of inflammation. Our results show a markedly decreased CYP2C19 activity during inflammation, irrespective of CYP2C19 genotype. The study illustrates the substantial effect of inflammation on voriconazole exposure in clinical practice. Hence, it is important to consider inflammatory status during voriconazole treatment, as patients with inflammation will require dose reductions. 24 , 25 , 26 We expect that this is not applicable for CYP2C19 predicted PMs, since for those patients, the predicted CYP2C19 activity might be too low to be inhibited. Unfortunately, in our cohort, no CYP2C19 predicted PMs were present, so we could not investigate the influence of inflammation on this group. Our results are in line with previous work showing a correlation between increased CRP levels and increased voriconazole levels. 23 , 26 , 29 , 30 , 31 Moreover, previous studies reported decreased voriconazole metabolic ratio and increased trough concentrations with increasing inflammation as quantified by CRP 23 , 26 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 or cytokine levels, 30 , 33 potentially resulting in supratherapeutic levels in patients with inflammation. 25

In our study, we explored the effect of inflammation on CYP2C19 activity for the different CYP2C19 genotypes and showed a difference in percentual CYP2C19 activity decrease for the different CYP2C19 predicted drug metabolizer phenotypes. The largest increase in dose‐corrected voriconazole level was observed for RMs (486%) and the smallest for NMs (245%). No difference in the effect of the extent of inflammation on CYP2C19 activity for the different CYP2C19 predicted drug metabolizer phenotypes was observed. We anticipated the largest effect of phenoconversion in IMs, because inhibition of decreased activity will result in a loss of enzyme function. This was previously shown for CYP2C19 inhibition by concurrent medication. 34 In this study, all IMs were converted to the PM status independent of the type of inhibitor (moderate or strong). For the UM, RM, and NM phenotypes the strength of the inhibitor affected the degree of the phenoconversion. Our data suggest that inflammation can be seen as a strong inhibitor influencing all CYP2C19 drug metabolizer phenotypes. This has the largest influence on RMs, due to their increased starting dose. Unfortunately, our data were too sparse to allow for detailed analysis of CYP2C19 activity for the specific CYP2C19 drug metabolizer phenotypes. In previous work with pediatric patients a heterogenous effect of CRP on voriconazole plasma concentration was reported for different CYP2C19 predicted drug metabolizer phenotypes. Concentrations for IMs increased from 17% to 39% with a CRP level increased to 20 mg/L, and from 37% to 75% for NMs with an increase in CRP level to 120 mg/L. 35 In our study, similar effects of increasing CRP levels on the voriconazole trough concentrations were observed in the different drug metabolizer phenotypes (Table S2).

In the subgroup analysis of eight patients with longitudinal data prior to and during inflammation, 16% of the voriconazole concentrations were outside of the therapeutic range (1–6 mg/L) (Figure S3). Interestingly, the 4% supratherapeutic measurements all occurred during increased CRP levels. Moreover, 50% of the supratherapeutic levels were found in RMs. This could be explained by the higher enzyme activity requiring a increased dose in the absence of inflammation, resulting in a higher risk of developing supratherapeutic levels when the CYP2C19 activity is inhibited during inflammation.

From a clinical perspective, our data suggest that once the adequate voriconazole dose for a particular patient has been established, frequent TDM may not be necessary. Only when CRP levels change frequent TDM is indicated (Figure 4 and Figure S3). For example, when the right dose has been established for a patient with inflammation and the infection is cleared, CRP may drop and a higher voriconazole dosage may be required to prevent subtherapeutic levels. This is in line with results from a study investigating patients receiving voriconazole in an intensive care unit. In these patients (n = 153), 54% of voriconazole levels were outside the target range. 36

In the current study, some assumptions were made. First, CRP levels were used as a proxy for inflammation. Ideally, IL‐6 levels are used since these are a more direct marker to assess inflammation. 37 A study utilizing hip surgery as a model for the effect of acute inflammation showed that during acute inflammation maximum IL‐6 levels are reached at day 1, while CRP levels peak at days 2 and 3. 18 CYP2C19 activity decreased on day 1 and the lowest level of CYP2C19 activity was measured at day 3. 18 These data show a comparable effect of acute inflammation on CYP2C19 activity and CRP levels. Secondly, we assumed steady‐state kinetics for voriconazole. In both studies used for data extraction, patients were treated for at least 24 h after two loading doses or received at least 10 doses of voriconazole. 11 , 26 This assumption is supported by evidence from literature and guidelines for TDM. 6 , 38 , 39 Thirdly, we used voriconazole dose corrected through levels as a proxy for CYP2C19 activity. While CYP2C19 is the most important enzyme in the metabolism of voriconazole, other enzymes such as CYP3A4 also play a role, such as CYP2C19, CYP3A4 which are also affected by genetic variation. 14 , 15 The most widely recognized and studied variant is CYP3A4*22 allele. 40 , 41 Carriers of at least one CYP3A4*22 allele have a significantly increased voriconazole C min‐to‐dose ratio. 42 However, the frequency of CYP3A4*22 is low with a minor allele frequency of 0.05. 43 , 44 Consequently, the majority of subjects is a predicted CYP3A4 NM 45 and it is safe to assume a similar effect of inflammation on CYP3A4 in the studied patients irrespective of their CYP3A4 genotype.

Our study was a post hoc analysis of two clinical studies which has limitations. First, the sample size was limited, and the number of available measurements varied considerably per patient. However, a sensitivity analysis indicated that the association between CRP and voriconazole level was not influenced by the number of measurements (Figures S1 and S2). Both of the studies used allowed the use of concomitant medication which could potentially influence CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 activity. For all patients, the concomitant use of known CYP2C19 interacting drugs was recorded. Concomitant drug use included pantoprazole, omeprazole, esomeprazole, and fluconazole or combinations of these drugs. Pantoprazole has a low enzymatic inhibitory effect on CYP2C19; therefore, only little effect on CYP2C19 activity is expected. 46 Omeprazole, esomeprazole, and fluconazole are moderate CYP2C19 inhibitors. Therefore, the inhibitory effect on voriconazole level is expected to be limited. 47 For the patients using fluconazole and omeprazole, the total inhibitory effect could influence the CYP2C19 activity. However, this group was too small to perform a subgroup analysis. In future research, it will be important to investigate the influence of concurrent medication on voriconazole trough levels more in‐depth. Particularly medication targeting IL‐6 by blocking the IL‐6 signaling pathway such as tocilizumab can have a profound effect on revering downregulation of CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 activity. 48 Finally, genotyping was restricted to CYP2C19 *2, *3 and *17. While these variants together represent >98% of the CYP2C19 variants in the Dutch population, the presence of rare genetic variants cannot be excluded and could have resulted in misclassification. 49
In conclusion, inflammation downregulates CYP2C19 activity. While this effect appears largest for CYP2C19 RMs, no clinically relevant differences were observed between the CYP2C19 genotypes.
